title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
description: Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.Germany's armed
body: Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems.A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police.It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement.German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks."We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said.Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich.The local police force has been contacted for comment.German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment ​and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries.The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022.However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles.After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement.A spate of drone sightings in European airspace last year left the continent on high alert, prompting the EU to discuss a continent-wide "drone wall" of air defences.Some European officials have blamed Russia for these drone sightings, claims Moscow has previously described as "absurd".

schema.headline: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident

title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
description: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled
body: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain."This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

schema.headline: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast

title: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court
description: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradi
body: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradited to the Republic of Ireland on SundayByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspondentEimear Flanagan and Barry O'ConnorBBC News NISuspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai.He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October.Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan arrived into Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin on the government jet on Sunday eveningThe US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other member of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing.Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police.He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis".'I won't be getting bail'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A police convoy escorted Kinahan at speed to the courtKinahan arrived at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, where gardaí arrested and charged him.He was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin.All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks.In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top.He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places.Image source, Mike O'DonnellImage caption, An artist's impression of Kinahan during his hearing on SundayKinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this.When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes."Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening.Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink.Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison.Judge McGrath explained to Kinahan he could file an application for bail through the High Court.Kinahan replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time."'Landmark of judicial cooperation'The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition."The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated.Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries".He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings".His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group.He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.What is the Kinahan cartel?According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities.The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza.A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr.Image source, CAROLINE QUINN/GETTY IMAGESImage caption, Gangland rivals tried to shoot Daniel Kinahan during a boxing weigh-in event in Dublin's Regency Hotel 10 years agoIn 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively.The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m.Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016.He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court

title: Why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many
description: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uni
body: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty."Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".They had been about to go on their honeymoon.But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers – Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole – will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more – at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.Some 6,000 prisoners had been due to be let out early under a law aimed at making space in the prisons system.Burnham paused that policy for a review after a public backlash, with particular focus on the possible release of two of PC Harper's killers after serving half rather than two-thirds of their sentences.But on Monday, while it was confirmed that about 1,000 prisoners would be excluded from the scheme, Bowers and Cole were not among them.Lissie described this as "disgraceful and disgusting", while PC Harper's mother said she was "devastated".A petition against their release has received more than 750,000 signatures.Long, the driver, is not eligible for early release.Recent weeks have shown just how much the case continues to stir strong emotions.Tiffany Lynch, chair of the National Police Federation of England and Wales, said that for rank and file officers up and down the country it "feels personal" – "there is disgust, upset"."We have a police officer who was four weeks into his marriage, dedicated to his job, responding to an incident of burglary, that our public expect of our police, has sacrificed his life in the line of duty and the people are not fulfilling their sentence," she said. "It just doesn't make sense."Stuart Blaik, the senior investigating officer in PC Harper's case, told BBC Breakfast his killers' early release was "particularly hard to understand" and would impact police morale.Justice Secretary Alex Norris has apologised to victims and their families and said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

schema.headline: Why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many

title: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
description: Image source, Alyssa GrocuttImage caption, Dr Alyssa Grocutt explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhDByEleanor LawrieSocial Affair
body: Image source, Alyssa GrocuttImage caption, Dr Alyssa Grocutt explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhDByEleanor LawrieSocial Affairs ReporterTattoos have been in the cultural mainstream for years. Even the prime minister has got one (a bee, on his bicep).And there are no signs the trend is starting to fade. More people than ever are going under the needle as a form of self-expression: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, according to a 2024 YouGov poll.The most popular body part to be inked? The upper arm, says YouGov.But has that acceptance carried over into the workplace?'I don't think it's totally accepted'Sociologist Dr Michael Rees says a big gulf in social acceptability remains between visible and non-visible tattoos, particularly those on  hands, neck and face as opposed to the rest of the body."I don't think it's completely accepted, and I think there's probably limits to that."While Rees himself has his hands and neck inked, he didn't get either done until he got his first permanent job as an academic."Even working in the career I work in, I was concerned that it may harm my job prospects."I think people getting tattooed in those areas are potentially restricting the careers that they go into."This is borne out by 2022 YouGov research, which found that while about two-thirds of people consider visible tattoos on the face or neck unprofessional, a similar proportion would think other visible tattoos are professional.Image source, Matthew ReesImage caption, Sociologist Dr Michael Rees has his hands and neck inked, but didn't get either done until he got his first permanent job as an academicDr Alyssa Grocutt, who is herself heavily tattooed, explored perceptions of tattoos in the workplace for her PhD at the University of Calgary in Canada, and found many stereotypes around tattooed people still exist today, both positive and negative.Perhaps unsurprisingly, people with intimidating tattoos – in this study, a skull and a knife – were perceived as risky, while those with "friendly" tattoos of a rose and some leaves were perceived as more creative and artistic.Overall, job applicants with visible tattoos are still slightly less likely to be hired than those without, she says.But for entrepreneurs, or those working in creative industries, Grocutt suggests they may be viewed as an extension of someone's personal brand."Even 11 years ago, when I started getting tattooed, the hands, neck and face were called 'job stoppers', and a lot of artists wouldn't tattoo people in those areas," she says."I think it's shifting a bit or maybe tattoo artists don't want to be gatekeepers. There's more positive perceptions now, [but] you still get a lot more attention, and that's an adjustment to get used to."From counterculture to mainstreamFor centuries, tattoos were firmly linked to criminal gangs and sailors and, more recently, counter-cultural movements such as punk and motorbike clubs.But since the early 2000s, tattoos have been steadily "demystified" through a combination of celebrities and popular TV shows such as Tattoo Fixers and London Ink, says Rees."When I got my first tattoos in the late '90s... they were outside of the mainstream. But they are everywhere now."Every tattooed person he interviewed in the 2000s for his research cited David Beckham as their inspiration; the footballer made a statement when he got his first inking in 1999. Now, celebs like Harry Styles and Ed Sheeran are covered in tattoos, with more than 50 each.'A more affordable way of becoming an art collector'Tattoo artist Martha Smith thinks stigma has "changed massively", with tattoos no longer seen as associated with criminality or class discrimination.And new trends are emerging too. Smith, who is based in Broadstairs, Kent, specialises in fine line and dot work tattoos. The hashtag #finelinetattoo has racked up 10.3m searches on Instagram, while #dotworktattoo boasts 4.8m searches."Probably until the early noughties, there was a very specific person who thought they could be tattooed. But in the 13 years I've been tattooing, clients have certainly become more diverse," Smith says, adding that she quite often tattoos NHS workers, social workers or teachers.Image source, Martha SmithImage caption, Tattoo artist Martha Smith specialises in fine line and dot work tattoos and thinks stigma has "changed massively"Catherine Hibbert, 44, waited almost 20 years to get her first tattoo. She now plans to get one every year of her forties."I was a bit nervous when I went for my first one," she says. "I was scared of it being painful, or that I was making the wrong decision.But as soon as the tattoo template was on, Hibbert says she "instantly loved it"."I guess it's an adrenaline rush, but I'm on a high for days after."Her forearm tattoo comprises geometric shapes symbolising different members and aspects of her family."They've all got meaning, and I like the fact that I can design them myself," says Hibbert, who works in an art gallery.Image source, Catherine HibbertImage caption, "I guess it's an adrenaline rush, but I'm on a high for days after," says Catherine Hibbert, who plans to get a tattoo every year of her forties  Smith thinks tattooists themselves now come from a much broader artistic background."You now often go to a tattooist because of their artwork. This massively opens up the kind of person that would want a tattoo and what a tattoo can mean. It also is a more affordable way of becoming an art collector."This chimes with how Hibbert feels."Everybody loves my arm tattoo," she says. "I think it's because it's quite unusual from what lots of people expect a tattoo to look like… this is very delicate."The value of authenticity Of all the factors behind tattoos' popularity, authenticity is the one Rees thinks trumps them all – because, he says, it is something we really value culturally."A lot of my respondents thought that was something that a tattoo gave them, a commitment to a band or to a person, to [addiction] recovery, just to kind of [being] who they really were."Of course, the elephant in the room is regret. Tattoos are permanent, and critics suggest that as these generations age they may no longer like the inkings they chose decades previously.But Hibbert says that is not a concern for her."They're like a story, so it's memories and it's stories about me and my life."

schema.headline: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers -  the case that Mathipa had been investigating.After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.Outside the UK watch on YouTube, externalThe case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer."When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

schema.headline: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC

title: The Hundred 2026 results: Sunrisers Leeds close to qualification after Welsh Fire win
description: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Car
body: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Carse 3-24Sunrisers Leeds won by 71 runsScorecard. TableSunrisers Leeds moved closer to securing qualification for The Hundred's knockout stages with a comprehensive 71-run win over Welsh Fire.Mitch Marsh, the tournament's leading run-scorer, struck his fourth half-century of the season for second-placed Sunrisers as they made 201-4 at Headingley.The Australian opener hit a 34-ball 50 and added 89 for the first wicket with Ryan Rickelton.Chris Woakes, who took 2-41, claimed the breakthrough when he had Rickelton caught for 40, while Harry Brook (23 from 11 balls) and Marsh fell within the space of five deliveries, caught off Jordan Clark and Lockie Ferguson respectively.Captain Zak Crawley struck four sixes in a 12-ball 34 as Sunrisers pressed on, while Dan Lawrence (29) and Matthew Revis (15) ended the innings with an unbroken partnership of 27.Fifth-placed Fire were unable to keep up with the required run-rate in their reply as only Matt Short (43) and Joe Root (31), who put on 49 for the second wicket, made more than 13.Short was one of three victims for Brydon Carse, who also removed opener Phil Salt (13) and Marco Jansen (1).Root was caught behind off Nathan Ellis, who also bowled Rachin Ravindra for two, while Jordan Cox also fell cheaply, caught for 12 off Matthew Potts.Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Woakes both finished unbeaten on 13 as Fire closed on 130-6, well short of their target having chosen to chase at the toss.Sunrisers now only need to avoid defeat against Manchester Super Giants on Tuesday to progress, while victory would put them in contention for top spot should leaders Trent Rockets lose against Southern Brave on Monday.Fire, who would have moved second with a win on Sunday, are the lowest placed of three teams on 16 points and will likely need success against London Spirit on Wednesday and then rely on net run-rate to secure the final knockout spot.The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleyBirmingham Phoenix 162-4 (100 balls): Clarke 73 (42), Dickson 51 (28); Crocombe 1-8London Spirit 166-3 (82 balls): Livingstone 66 (30), Brevis 55 (31); Thompson 1-24London Spirit won by seven wicketsScorecard. TableDewald Brevis and Liam Livingstone shared a 103-run partnership as London Spirit beat Birmingham Phoenix by seven wickets at Lord's.In a match between two eliminated sides, Livingstone hit 66 from 30 balls, while Brevis struck an unbeaten 55 from 31 as Spirit passed their target of 163 with 18 balls to spare.Coming together at 43-2 after the hosts had lost Jonny Bairstow and Lhuan-dre Pretorius for 10 and 16 respectively, the pair struck a collective total of 12 fours and seven sixes, hitting the ball deep into the stands on multiple occasions.Home captain Livingstone skied a catch to Sean Dickson off Tom Helm, but Brevis saw Spirit home alongside James Coles (9), striking back-to-back fours to first reach his half-century and then end the match.Phoenix reached what appeared to be a competitive score after being put into bat, with opener Joe Clarke scoring 73 from 42 deliveries and Dickson hitting an unbeaten 51 from 28.The pair put on a third-wicket stand of 92 after Mitch Owen, Joe Weatherley and Laurie Evans had all fallen for single figures, while Clarke ultimately departed from the 91st ball of the innings, caught by Livingstone off Henry Crocombe.Phoenix's sixth defeat in seven matches mean they stay bottom of The Hundred standings, while Spirit moved level with sixth-placed Southern Brave on eight points, but remain beneath them by virtue of an inferior net run-rate.Nottingham is the venue for Monday's action in The Hundred with Trent Rockets hosting Southern Brave.The match for the women's side at 15:00 BST is a top-of-the-table clash, with leaders Rockets aiming to clinch their place in the Lord's final.Victory over Brave in their final match would secure their spot, although given they have a superior net run-rate they could go directly to Lord's even if they lose.Second-placed Brave are in a strong position to secure a place in the Eliminator - and would be certain if they win.The Rockets' men's side will also secure their spot in the final on 16 August with victory over Brave in their match which gets under way at 18:00.Brave are playing for pride, having already been eliminated and victory would guarantee they avoid the wooden spoon.You can follow ball-by-ball commentary on both matches on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

title: Family of Kaylan Hippsley devastated as killer Harley Whiteman to be freed early
description: Julie Craig, Kaylan's cousin, said the news had left the family "devastated".She said they had received a phone call from the victim support team two
body: Julie Craig, Kaylan's cousin, said the news had left the family "devastated".She said they had received a phone call from the victim support team two weeks ago, informing them there was going to be a change to Whiteman's prison conditions."We've had a letter from the prison service, saying his sentence is being reviewed as part of the Sentencing Act 2026, where there's been a remodel, and as a result of that his sentence has been reduced to four years, of which he has to serve at least half," Craig said. She said this meant Whiteman could be released under licence in the autumn."It beggar's belief that after two years he's allowed back into the community," she said."It's absolutely devastating. Kaylan's grandmother, who is his legal guardian, she is absolutely distraught. She's been unable to return to the home she shared with him."This just feels like a kick in the teeth."Craig said she wanted the decision to be reversed."I understand there needs to be changes because the prisons are full to capacity. But that's not the victims' fault," she said."Harley Whiteman will come out, he'll have the rest of his life to live."But Kaylan was only 13. I want them to take that into consideration when they're making these decisions. It's just wrong."If it means building new prisons, then that's what they need to do."She said the family "promised" Kaylan they would get justice for him, and had started a petition calling for Whiteman to be denied early release from prison.A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said it wanted to "block more offenders from getting out sooner into their sentence", but that could not happen without "risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing"."If that happened, police could not make arrests, courts could not remand offenders and there would be unchecked criminality on our streets," it added."We are pulling every lever to protect the public and cut crime – building prison places at the fastest rate since the Victorian era, launching the biggest ever expansion of tagging to toughen community punishment and increasing support to victims, giving them a say in the strict licence conditions of offenders."

schema.headline: Family of Kaylan Hippsley devastated as killer Harley Whiteman to be freed early

title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
description: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says
body: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97. Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms. Because every school sets its own uniform policy, parents can still face very different expectations and costs.Lorraine, who lives in London, has two children in secondary schools and is frustrated that her school has not changed any of its uniform policy this year.She says several items are still compulsory, including the branded blazer, tie, branded polo shirt, branded shorts and two-toned PE socks.Even the plain grey trousers or skirt have to be purchased from one of the school's suppliers, she says.Both her sons have been through a growth spurt this summer, so she is expecting to spend more than £200 on their branded items alone."I'm just frustrated, for me it's not even about the money," she says."I feel these inconsistencies do not make a difference to education and are really blinkered."But mum-of-five Carol, from Stockport, welcomes the changes at her children's school. She says her son's secondary school only requires a branded blazer, a branded jumper and tie, with everything else available from a range of shops.She tries to get most of her children's uniforms second-hand anyway, but always buys the blazer, which costs around £30, as she likes them to have a new one.She says anything that makes it more affordable for parents is a good thing.But others are not seeing the changes they would like.One father from Oxfordshire, who did not want to be named, says his daughter still has to have seven branded items - three for the uniform, three for PE and a summer polo shirt - as there are no alternatives allowed. "It's ridiculous and unfair. We are paying £200 which we can't afford," he says.Most primary schools already have very few branded items.At Broadhurst Primary, in North Manchester, only the school jumper – and, from 2027, the PE T-shirt – are branded, which the school says brings the total cost of its uniform to £13 per child.Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government survey.The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.Its general secretary Pepe Di'Iasio says schools are already trying to balance the cost to parents with maintaining a sense of identity. He says it's also important to keep expensive fashion brands out so no one feels excluded.Some schools have been phasing their changes in over the last few years.King's Oak Academy, in Bristol, has one compulsory item left on its uniform list - a branded PE T-shirt.The school, which goes from reception right through to Year 11, used to have a branded jumper, tie and a shirt, which together cost about £41.Students are now asked to wear a plain polo shirt - which changes colour for the lower, middle and upper school - a sweatshirt or cardigan, and grey skirt or trousers, with all pupils also wearing black trainers. The school says it now costs about £10 to £25, depending on where parents buy the uniform.

schema.headline: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules

title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
description: Image source, Johan PerssonImage caption, The stories of Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and Lyanna Stark are brought to life in the stage showByIan YoungsCu
body: Image source, Johan PerssonImage caption, The stories of Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and Lyanna Stark are brought to life in the stage showByIan YoungsCulture reporterThe first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".Image source, Johan PerssonImage caption, Michael Shaeffer plays the "mad king" of the play's title, Aerys II TargaryenThe Game of Thrones origin story is epic in both ambition and execution – it has taken seven years to reach the stage, clocks in at three hours 45 minutes, and features a 36-strong cast.The characters include younger versions of familiar figures like Ned Stark, Jaime Lannister and Robert Baratheon; and others whose fates were key to the events in the main saga, such as Lyanna Stark, Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and the "mad king" himself, Aerys II Targaryen.After opening in Shakespeare's home town, the RSC will hope it can go on to replicate the success of other spin-off plays like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Stranger Things: The First Shadow, which have both had lengthy runs in the West End and on Broadway.The Shakespeare connection stems from the fact Martin's novels were heavily inspired by Shakespeare's history plays, especially those about the battles between the houses of Lancaster and York during the Wars of the Roses in the 15th Century.Game of Thrones' US creator was heavily involved in the play, stationing a representative in rehearsals at all times, and he attended the opening night in Stratford on Saturday.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, George RR Martin travelled to Stratford-upon-Avon for the play's opening nightIn his review, the Guardian's Mark Lawson wrote, external: "Purists will object that, rather than staging Shakespeare-adjacent populist spin-offs, the RSC should be offering its house dramatist's royal dramas plain."The counter argument is that hitching on to a cultural juggernaut may bring in new sources of income and audiences."Audiences will respond differently to the play depending on whether they are already loyal Game of Thrones fans, which Lawson's four-star rating reflected."This feels like a five-star production for most devoted throners but a three-star for those who haven't seen the TV series," he said.Metro's critic Dave Freak agreed, external, also bestowing four stars."As a stand-alone piece of theatre, The Mad King scrapes through," he wrote. "But as an extension of the Game of Thrones world, it scores well, shifting the narrative to the stage with suitably theatrical thrust."'Lacks grit, gore and nudity'The Telegraph's Dominic Cavendish wrote, external: "At almost four hours, it's a long evening, sometimes too dense with detail, and it lacks the grit and gore (not to mention the nudity) of the TV series."Still, it capably serves newbies and devotees, and speaks in a timely fashion to our age of unruly leaders."He added: "It's not up there, yet, with the Harry Potter or Stranger Things prequels but, on balance, the Game of Thrones franchise has yet another worthwhile and lucrative spin-off on its hands."The Times' critic Clive Davis, external had greater reservations, writing that while the play "gives hardcore GoT fans a chance to go hunting for 'Easter eggs', it seldom comes close to matching the grim aura of the TV series"."Duncan Macmillan's script is sorely lacking in poetry. Events plod forward, one after the other, and although Michael Shaeffer is a thoroughly compelling presence as the cruel and chronically unstable monarch Aerys, other performances seem nuance-free. Too many lines are simply shouted. You expect better of the RSC."Davis concluded: "It goes without saying that there are more than enough GoT devotees to keep the box office ticking over for the rest of eternity, but only the most dedicated of them will have the energy for this marathon."Image source, Johan PerssonImage caption, Elizabeth Ayodele as Princess Elia Martell and Tanisha Spring as Ashara DayneOthers were more enthusiastic, and Whatsonstage's Sarah Crompton's five-star review, external said the play is "a triumph; a soaring, surging spectacle and a latter-day history play, both serious and popular".She added: "It is a remarkable achievement, wonderfully directed by [Dominic] Cooke and superbly acted by every member of the 35-strong ensemble. The result is a brilliant exhibition of how theatre can create magic."The Independent's Alice Saville, external, awarding four stars, said the "stellar stage show has all the thrillingly staged battles, gory deaths and, yes, dragons that the most bloodthirsty fan could hope for"."But there's also a surprising amount of heart – of the warm, still-beating kind – as it lingers on the faces of its fallen," she said.Image source, Johan PerssonThe play begins more than a decade before the events in the first book and TV series, opening with the tourney at Harrenhal, a great jousting tournament where the houses of the Seven Kingdoms gathered and where key events in the Game of Thrones legend took place.Macmillan said he wanted to create something "on the scale of a Shakespearean tragedy and a Shakespearean history".The playwright told BBC News: "The challenge was writing something for a fan base who take this world and their characters very, very seriously and know so much about it, and also the complete newbies, and writing something that is going to work for both of those people."Making something that is going to knock the socks off of everybody has been a real challenge. It's taken a long time, but I think we've got there."Image source, Johan PerssonImage caption, Michael Abubakar (right) plays a young Eddard 'Ned' StarkCooke said there were "lots of similarities" with Shakespeare, especially themes of "dynastic struggle, what it means to have power, intergenerational conflict and powerful families".Martin has been "very supportive" in the process of creating the play, the director added."He's been collaborative in terms of the development of the script. We've worked very closely with him. And George, I think, picked up quite quickly that we were very serious about honouring what he'd done."Tamara Harvey, the RSC's co-artistic director, said: "George himself talks about how Shakespeare and the Wars of the Roses inspired him to write these stories."So the connections feel very deep, and of course themes are shared: power, love, succession, battles for who gets to rule who – it's all there in the Shakespeare history, just as it is in Game of Thrones."Asked about future plans for the play, Harvey replied: "We're hoping as many people as possible get to see it, and that starts here in Stratford. And from then, who knows?"

schema.headline: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare

title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
description: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge
body: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge SandemanOn Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, The view towards the sky from the hill in Galicia where Mark hopes to capture the total eclipseHe's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.But this is his first total solar eclipse."I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him."I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory Phillips-Brown flew from upstate New York to Iceland to see the eclipseThis will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago."It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomenon more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation."They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory booked their flights and camper van more than a year agoThe path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says."What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew."We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."Image source, Andrew WillsImage caption, Andrew Wills is travelling to Majorca with his wife and 90-year-old father to see the eclipseHe has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon."We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago."We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer."And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph."We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

schema.headline: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world

title: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing
description: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She
body: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes. For example, depending on available places:If I get AAA, then I could do physics at SussexBBC could be physics at AberystwythCCD could be physics at Nottingham TrentThe Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher. She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people. At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades". On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history. "The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says."That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day. That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade."You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says."Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact. "Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says."With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your results. But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website. "I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand. On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it."It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford. "All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available. "Work up a priority list," he says."For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person. She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities. "I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says."You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.

schema.headline: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing

title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
description: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th Century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs
body: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th Century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install"."It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.Image source, Blenheim PalaceImage caption, The original plans for the parterre at Blenheim show its scaleBut the garden was dismantled in 1760, only leaving its outline to be revealed in spells of particularly hot weather."The footprint of it has appeared out on the lawn, and it is absolutely fantastic - it's a huge structure, it's just massive," Mills said."We know it's there, we know it's under the ground, we know the archaeology is there and it's just one of those happy coincidences of this very, very hot weather that these things appear.""It's just superb to see - it's amazing."Image source, National TrustImage caption, The outlines of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames - have also been uncoveredElsewhere in Oxfordshire, the weather has also revealed the outline of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames.The parch marks show a range of 16th Century buildings which had once stood on the National Trust property's Oval Lawn.Archeological enquiries at the site in recent years have discovered that the outlines belonged to a long, narrow building which once stood on the lawn and linked two sides of a medieval courtyard.Image source, English HeritageImage caption, The footprint of a Tudor storehouse at Portchester Castle has been revealed by the warm weatherMeanwhile, at Portchester Castle in Hampshire, the warm conditions have led to parch marks revealing the outline of a Tudor storehouse.English Heritage, which runs the castle, said the storehouse was believed to date from between 1489 and 1540.Image source, National TrustImage caption, Parch marks at Mottisfont show the remains of 13th and 16th Century wall foundationsMottisfont, near Romsey, has also experienced similar marks this summer - uncovering the remains of 13th and 16th Century wall foundations.The National Trust said the walls were the "buried remains of monastery buildings including a cloister and various other buildings, as well as later Tudor alterations".Archaeologist James Brown said the outlines were "intriguing glimpses into the oldest history of buildings known" at Mottisfont."We have carried out some geophysical surveys but the buildings have never been dug so their secrets remain hidden except for these rare moments when their outlines appear in the lawns," he added.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South

title: Harry Potter fans force power link diversion to avoid Dobby's grave

body: He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave"."I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation,  but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.
